Complex weather scenario developing over the next
few days will result in an active start to the work week for
Southeast Arizona. This primarily revolves around the tropical 
activity across the eastern Pacific and an amplified trough off
the West Coast. The first tropical feature is defined by the 
NHC at 8 PM MST SAT as Hurricane Odalys, which is a category 1 
system with maximum sustained winds 80 mph near 21.1N/123.6W 
moving N at 6 kts. The second tropical feature defined by the 
NHC at 11 PM MST SAT is Hurricane Polo, which is a category 3 
system with maximum sustained winds of 120 mph near 19.8N/113.4W
moving NW at 9 kts.

Odalys will continue to move slowly north over cooler waters 
today, weakening to a tropical storm by 28/00Z this afternoon 
near 22.4N/123.1W. The latest water vapor imagery is showing the
middle to upper portions of this feature already shearing NE 
into southern California this morning along the SERN periphery 
of the upper trough along the West Coast. The latest GOES water
vapor imagery indicated a dry airmass across SE AZ, with PWATs
generally between 0.50-0.90 inches. Deeper moisture (PWATs 1.50+
inches) observed on this imagery along and west of the NRN Baja
MX associated with the sheared off mid and upper portions of 
Hurricane Odalys. As the trough digs to the SE today, it will 
shunt this moisture into SW by 28/00Z this afternoon with the 
plume extending into central AZ by 28/06Z this evening. We will
start to see significant mid and high clouds expand from west to
east as the day progresses, with a few light showers west of 
Tucson late this afternoon into tonight. With the lower-levels 
still dry today, virga will be evident with a few gusts to 30 
mph near the evaporating downdrafts.

Polo is much stronger and closer than Odalys to our neck of the
woods so it will have a more significant impact of moistening- 
up SE AZ. Polo is progged to move northwest today but will
quickly recurve to the NE as the upper trough moves closer. Polo
will weaken to a category 1 between the Baja Spur and tip of 
the Baja by 5 PM MST Monday afternoon. This track will help 
push tropical moisture northward up the Gulf of California 
today and across all of southern Arizona Monday and Tuesday. 
The 27/00Z GEFS and ECMWF ensemble means still indicate a plume
of moist PWATs 2.5-3.5 standard deviations above normal across 
Southeast Arizona by 29/00Z Monday afternoon. The GEFS ensemble
mean is less with regards to the moisture than the ECMWF
ensemble mean. Polo itself is still NOT expected to impact us 
directly. The official track by the NHC has Polo becoming a 
remnant low in east-central Sonora Mexico near the 
Sonora/Chihuahua border at 5 PM MST Tuesday afternoon. 

Our main event is still expected to behave more like a fall-like 
synoptic system utilizing the tropical moisture available across
our area. The upper pattern will focus a deformation axis out
ahead of the trough this afternoon/tonight, oriented SW-NE from
the northern Baja into central Arizona. Originally, weak 
vorticity aloft will move through this axis resulting in weak 
showers. However, as we move into the evening, a modest lower-
level (850-700 mb) moisture flux convergence will feed moisture 
into this area increasing the coverage and intensity of the 
showers, but it will also tend to allow showers the train as new
storms will form toward the deeper moisture despite individual 
storms moving rapidly toward the NE. The impact of this will 
generally avoid SE AZ tonight, but will start to move into the 
western portions of the forecast area Monday morning. 

The trough tries to become neutrally oriented Monday,
establishing a more broad diffluence area aloft across the 
eastern portions of the CWA (east of Tucson) Monday afternoon. 
This will increase the coverage of showers and thunderstorms. 
Deformation across all of Southeast Arizona will then increase 
Monday night and eventually phase with the remnants of Polo 
moving NE through Sonora/Chihuahua Mexico Tuesday. Strong
dynamics and deep moisture in place will result in widespread 
showers and thunderstorms Monday night into Tuesday. Strong 
moisture flux convergence will continue to allow for storms to 
train, increasing the potential for heavy rain along the band of
precipitation that develop. Strong 0-6km bulk shear Tuesday 
will bring about the potential for mini-supercells to be 
embedded within the widespread storm activity, especially to the
SE of Tucson.

Although rainfall rates may not be as impressive as we see 
during the heart of the Monsoon season, this rainfall may be 
more widespread and become problematic with time as rainfall 
runoff struggles to drain into normally dry washes, roadway dips
and other low-lying areas. Training storms will result in
localized flash flooding issues. The WPC has all of Southeast 
Arizona highlighted in a SLGT Risk of excessive rainfall Monday
